newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia appeased by Howard attack on Australia racism.
newsitem.headline: Asia appeased by Howard attack on Australia racism.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard appears to have stuck a pin into a bubble of Asian anger by firmly speaking out last week against racism in his country.
There has only been a muted response in Asian nations so far to Howard's speech denouncing the country's race row politician Pauline Hanson.
Most comment has been favourable although some questions have been asked about why it took the Australian prime minister so long to speak out as forthrightly as he did.
Howard, initially reluctant to respond to Hanson's anti-immigrant remarks following her election to national parliament last year, went on the offensive last Thursday.
He accused her of exploiting feelings of fear and instability in Australia.
Indonesia's leading Kompas newspaper said in an article on Saturday that Howard's speech was strong, clear and worthy of praise.
"Hanson will be detrimental for Australia, because basically Australia needs the Asia Pacific just like the region needs Australia," it said.
"Maybe we, who are in this Asia Pacific region, can help this confused neighbour (Australia) by embracing it, even though it is hurtful to listen to Hanson's empty talk," said the article.
The English-language Observer newspaper said Hanson clearly had an "abhorrence of any racial strain that does not correspond to the Anglo-Saxon one that flows through her veins."
But the newspaper said that it had no doubt that Howard planned to counteract the "Pauline Hanson syndrome".
In Seoul, a South Korean foreign ministry official said he believed Howard spoke out strongly enough but wondered if his response should not have been made earlier.
"Howard's lukewarm attitude allowed the issue to develop in this way," said the official who asked not to be identified.
He said there no signs that the racial discrimination issue had harmed bilateral economic ties between Australia and South Korea.
"I don't think the row in Australia had any major impact in our country. I don't see any South Korean tourists cancelling their Australian destinations," he said.

In Japan, where there has been a drop off in tourism to Australia unconnected to the race issue, a travel industry official said Australians needed to keep up their pressure to stamp out any signs of racism.
Some analysts noted that Howard's strong speech was made the week after a visit to Australia by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

The analysts said there was no suggestion that Hashimoto raised the race issue in a formal way. But as Australia's main trading partner, Japanese views on the issue would be carefully listened to, they said.
An article in Thailand's newspaper The Nation also took Howard to task for waiting so long to speak out.

"Howard opted to remain silent when Hanson's maiden speech sparked a national furore, claiming that it was all about free speech. But if he was truly opposed to racism, he should have exercised his own freedom of speech and condemned Hanson," the article said.
"That Howard has chosen now to condemn Hanson reeks of self-interest."
The article said Asia can do without Australia, but Australia cannot do without Asia.
"Australia should be told in no uncertain terms that Asians do not do business with bigots, send our children to be educated by racists or visit a country where Asians are likely to be spat at.
"But in so doing, we must also condemn the racists in our midst. Otherwise, like Howard, we risk being dismissed as mere hypocrites."
